Mining · Haut-Katanga and Lualaba

What is changing on your mining perimeter, date by date

We map pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, structures and tracks inside and around your mining perimeter, and flag what has changed from one date to the next. Houses, fields and water points within the distances of Mining Code art. 279 are inventoried with their dates. The survey is done remotely, from satellite imagery, and an analyst checks every result.

Request a proposal Mining Code art. 279

The problem, in your words

A perimeter fixed on paper, ground that keeps moving

“Our teams can no longer reach part of the perimeter.”

When access to the ground closes, you still need to know what is happening there: how many new pits, how much disturbed ground, which tracks have opened since the last visit.

“New pits appear from one season to the next.”

Artisanal workings move. A dated map of the sites that exist, and of those that appear, gives land and HSE teams a shared starting point.

“Houses and fields are close to the planned works.”

Mining Code art. 279 sets distances that protect houses, fields and villages against mining occupation. Before a pit or a waste dump is extended, you need to know what lies within them.

“The expansion has to be preceded by a census.”

Where people would be displaced, the Mining Code requires compensation and resettlement first. A dated record prepares the census and fixes what existed at the cut-off date.

Who uses it

  • Land and community relations departments
  • HSE and environment managers
  • Geology, survey and GIS teams
  • Social performance managers
  • ESIA and RAP consultancies
  • Lenders and independent monitors

Artisanal workings and excavations

Pits, disturbed ground and spoil, from one date to the next

We map pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations inside your mining right and in a band around it, and flag new sites between dates. Each change is flagged automatically and confirmed by an analyst, with before-and-after views. The tracks leading to the sites are mapped with them.

In the rainy season, when cloud often hides the ground, radar comparisons show the larger changes even under cloud cover; the areas they flag are then checked on an optical image or, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, by drone.

What we map is the ground. We do not identify, count or follow anyone, and underground workings and covered shafts cannot be seen from space. A flag shows where to look; on its own it proves nothing, and what to do about it is your decision.

Artisanal mining zones

A zone d’exploitation artisanale (ZEA) is created by ministerial arrêté after consulting, among others, the provincial governor and the Cadastre Minier. A perimeter covered by a valid title cannot be turned into a ZEA, and only members of approved cooperatives may work in one (Mining Code, arts 109 to 111).

A dated map of pits on both sides of a boundary documents the state of the ground before and after a zone is created.

Structures nearby

Article 279: what lies within 800 and 1,000 metres of your works

Checked against the published texts on 27 September 2026. The summaries on this page are for orientation; they are not legal advice.

Article 279 of the Mining Code, as amended by Loi n° 18/001 of 9 March 2018, sets out the land a mining right holder may not occupy without consent.

Without the consent of the owner or lawful occupant, nobody may occupy land within:

  • 1,000 m of houses or buildings, whether “occupés, inoccupés ou temporairement inoccupés” (occupied, unoccupied or temporarily unoccupied);
  • 800 m of land hoed and ploughed for farm crops;
  • 800 m of a cattle farm, a reservoir, a hydroelectric dam or a private water reserve.

Without the consent of the competent authorities, nobody may occupy, among others, land within 800 m of a village, town or city, within 500 m of a hydroelectric dam or a State building, close to national defence installations, forming part of an airport or reserved for a railway project, nor a street, road or motorway, a national park or a tourist site. The governor may also set protection perimeters.

These distances protect occupants against mining occupation. They do not make a house built near a mine unlawful. The 2018 amendment widened them considerably: the 1,000 m distance from houses was 180 m in the 2002 text, and the 800 m distance from cultivated land was 45 m.

What you receive

  • A list of the houses and buildings within 1,000 m of the planned work area, each with its coordinates, its distance and the image date
  • The cultivated fields, water points and villages within 800 m
  • Structures that are new or gone since the previous survey, confirmed by an analyst
  • A table by band and by sector of the perimeter, and GIS files for your teams

Deciding what is permitted, and whose consent to seek, is for you and the competent authorities. Our inventory says what stands where, and since when the imagery shows it.

Before any relocation

Article 281: compensate and resettle first

Since 2018, art. 281 of the Mining Code has read: “En cas de déplacement des populations, l’opérateur minier est tenu préalablement de procéder à l’indemnisation, à la compensation et à la réinstallation des populations concernées.” Where people are displaced, the mining operator must first compensate and resettle them. Occupation that deprives rightful users of the land, or leaves it unfit for farming, gives a right to fair compensation; if no amicable settlement is reached, the matter can be taken to court after three months.

A dated record supports the census and the asset inventory; it does not replace them. We produce a register of the structures in the expansion footprint at the cut-off date, each with an ID, coordinates, the image date and a category (main building, outbuilding, enclosure, under construction), then the changes between the cut-off date and the census. Categories describe what the imagery shows; they establish neither use, ownership nor value.

Cut-off dates and resettlement plans

Where lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5 or the World Bank’s ESS5, the dated register supports the cut-off-date records.

Concession encroachment surveys

What stands inside your title, and in a band around it

We list the structures inside your boundaries and in a band around them, map new structures, cleared ground and tracks at the boundary between dates, and produce a structure layer for the whole permit for your land teams. Fences and barriers are too thin to be detected automatically on satellite imagery: an analyst checks them on drone imagery where it exists.

We work from the boundaries you supply and verify neither title nor land rights. Mining title perimeters can be viewed on the Cadastre Minier (CAMI) map portal.

Structures in the zones you define

Structures inside the zones your engineers define, such as the area downstream of a tailings facility, a blast radius or a flood line. We model neither dam breaks nor blasts; the zone comes from your studies.

Settlement growth

How built-up areas around your permit and installations change year by year, to show where pressure on land is rising.

What was built, cleared or dug on a parcel, and roughly when, from the satellite archive available for the place.

ESIA, audits and records

A dated initial state, and records that support your processes

The ESIA initial state

Décret n° 14/019 of 2 August 2014 requires a prior environmental and social impact study for any mining project, including “l’inventaire précis et détaillé de l’état initial du site, de son environnement naturel, socio-économique et humain” (art. 19): a precise and detailed inventory of the site’s natural, socio-economic and human initial state. Approval takes the form of a Certificat Environnemental, and an audit comes before its renewal. A dated register of structures, fields and land cover around the site feeds that initial state and lets you compare it from one audit to the next.

Dated records

Dated imagery, structure registers and maps, packaged with a fingerprint of each file and an independent timestamp, to show what was on the ground and when. These packs support legal and community processes; how the facts are characterised remains a matter for the authorities and the courts.

Evidence packs

How it works

From the boundaries of your title to a checked register

  1. Scope

    You send the permit boundaries and any planned work areas, and tell us what the register is for. We agree the distances, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Survey

    Satellite imagery, dated where the purpose requires it, and open building datasets give a first register of structures, pits and disturbed ground.

  3. Check

    An analyst confirms, corrects and adds to every result. Anything the imagery cannot settle is listed for your teams to verify on the ground.

  4. Deliver and repeat

    The report and GIS files go to the contacts you name. Re-surveys follow the agreed schedule, with a change notice after each one.

What we do, and what we don't

An honest scope

What we do

  • Map pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps, tracks and structures visible from above
  • Inventory what lies within the art. 279 distances, with the image date
  • Flag changes between dates, confirmed by an analyst
  • Work remotely, with no site access

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people
  • See underground workings or verify titles
  • Decide what is permitted, or stand in for the census
  • Work in the provinces outside our scope

The same method, for every country: mining · excavation mapping · concession and boundary surveys

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging on our perimeter?

No. We map the ground: pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations, tracks and structures, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by an analyst. We never identify, count or follow people.

Can you see shafts and underground workings?

No. Underground workings and covered shafts cannot be seen from above. We see what the surface shows: a pit opening, the spoil around it, water collecting in it and the tracks that lead to it.

Can you survey part of the perimeter our teams can no longer reach?

Yes, by satellite: the survey needs neither site access nor an overflight. No drone survey is offered over an occupied or contested area.

Can your survey stand in for the census before a relocation?

No. A dated record of structures and fields supports the census and asset inventory that Mining Code art. 281 and lenders’ standards require before any relocation; it does not replace them. Categories describe what the imagery shows; compensation needs verification on the ground.

Can you confirm the boundaries of our permit?

No. We work from the boundaries you give us, such as the coordinates in your title, and we do not verify title or land rights. Mining titles can also be viewed on the Cadastre Minier’s map portal.

Is remote analysis for a mine caught by the subcontracting law?

Assume that it is. ARSP’s sector guide treats externalised mining research, sampling and feasibility studies as subcontracting, and the law covers any service a company needs to carry out its main activity. That is why AfriScan works as a technology supplier to an eligible Congolese company; whether that arrangement is enough, given art. 7 on second-tier subcontractors, is a point for counsel. See subcontracting in the DRC.

Will images of our perimeter be published?

No. We never publish a client’s route, imagery or results without written permission, and the registers carry no names of people.

Send us your perimeter boundaries

The coordinates in your title or a boundary file (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), any planned work areas, and the dates that matter to you. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
